drops.title: Drop 002
drops.blurb: Five doorways. One of them has been played thirty one times in its entire life.

tracks.title: Protest (Live at Abbey Road)
tracks.why: A Manchester piano trio playing what sounds like electronic music performed by hand, recorded in the room where the Beatles made most of their records. Not rare, just quietly skipped by anyone who has decided they do not like jazz.

tracks.title: F*ck This Song
tracks.why: Nerdcore, the corner of rap that grew out of conventions and message boards rather than any city's scene. It is a joke record that is genuinely well built, which is the harder of the two things to pull off.

tracks.title: Talkin' Like You (Two Tall Mountains)
tracks.why: Recorded on a home tape machine in Greenwich Village years before anyone was calling this singer-songwriter music. She never got a record out, quit, and in 1974 packed a car and drove off. Nobody has seen her since.

tracks.title: cure
tracks.why: Not objectively rare or forgotten, but lesser known to western audiences. Japanese indie rock with an element reminiscent of midwest emo in the mix. (From Don't Laugh It Off, the trio's fifth album, October 2025.)

tracks.title: Fly Guy
tracks.why: Nine thousand plays for a duo who have been quietly putting out records for years without anybody deciding they are a thing yet. Funk, rap and a sense of humour, which is a combination most people get wrong.

tracks.title: Whalebones
tracks.why: Philadelphia, and a band who treat a song like a junk drawer: horns, clattering percussion, a voice that sounds like it is being dragged somewhere. It should collapse and it never quite does.

drops.title: Drop 001
drops.blurb: Six doors. Ten minutes of guitar recorded in 1971, German machine punk with seven thousand plays, and a band from Dallas with mariachi horns and a body count.

tracks.title: Maggot Brain
tracks.why: George Clinton reportedly told Eddie Hazel to play like he had just learned his mother died, then wiped most of the band out of the mix. What is left is ten minutes of guitar and almost nothing else. Every guitarist you like has heard this. Almost nobody else has.

tracks.title: Tell Me
tracks.why: A Chicago trio, one album on Secretly Canadian in 2006, gone not long after. People who reviewed it at the time called it a break up record, and the voice on it does sound like a man who has been shouting somewhere else all night.

tracks.title: Something Dangerous
tracks.why: Industrial pop with the pop left in, which is rarer than it sounds. Seventeen thousand views, and the kind of thing streaming services will happily play after it if you let them.

tracks.title: Too Old to Die Young
tracks.why: Delta slide blues out of Louisiana, and you have probably already heard it without knowing: Tarantino put it in Django Unchained. Almost nobody went looking for the rest of the record afterwards.

tracks.title: Drink with the Living Dead
tracks.why: Dallas, formed in 1999 by a man who calls himself Count Lyle and came out of a doom metal band. Horror punk crossed with spaghetti western, complete with mariachi horns. In 2002 a horror film used four of their songs and rewrote the script to give them a cameo.

tracks.title: Co Co Pino
tracks.why: German electronic punk from the turn of the eighties, made by people who had decided guitars were finished. Seven thousand plays. Half the machine music you have heard since owes it something, and almost nobody goes back to the source.
